summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The conversation began with the person noting it was Thursday and expressing they were having a difficult time emotionally, though they quickly pivoted to a technical project. They are building a full-featured TOTP authenticator app — essentially a Microsoft Authenticator replacement — with the core distinguishing feature being persistent, portable encrypted vault storage so that losing a device doesn't mean losing all 2FA accounts. The desired target platforms were all of the above: web PWA, desktop, mobile, and CLI for a Linux machine referred to as "JadeBox."

Claude built the full application across the conversation, starting with RFC 4226/6238-compliant TOTP/HOTP cryptographic core (base32 encoding, HMAC-SHA1/256/512, time-window math), then an AES-256-GCM encrypted vault using PBKDF2-SHA256 key derivation at 200,000 iterations. The web PWA was constructed with IndexedDB persistence, lock/unlock screens, account list with live countdown rings, manual entry, otpauth:// URI paste, camera QR scanning via jsQR, QR code generation via QRCode.js for account export/migration, vault export/import as encrypted JSON backup files, and password change functionality. A service worker was added for full offline capability. Testing used Playwright driving headless Chromium: all 10 end-to-end checks passed including TOTP math verified against official RFC vectors, vault encryption round-trips, persistence across reloads, wrong-password rejection, and encrypted export. The generated QR codes were independently decoded using pyzbar (zbar library) and confirmed to correctly encode the account secret and issuer. The camera scan-to-add flow was tested using a fake Y4M video feed containing a real QR code fed into Chromium's fake camera device.

The second part of the conversation involved a separate practical problem: the person's iPhone screen replacement rendered the phone non-functional (worked before the new screen, dead after), and they needed access to calls, texts, and their Amazon account while the primary device was unusable. The phone uses eSIM only with no SIM tray. An alternative phone was available but locked to a different carrier and not paid off. Claude worked through the eSIM transfer and call forwarding options, then identified the actual immediate need: accessing Amazon to track replacement parts. The real blocker turned out to be Amazon requiring a one-time passcode sent to the non-functional phone number even on devices already authenticated, which the person described accurately as "as many factors as stops you authentication." Claude advised going directly to Amazon's live chat support from an already-logged-in session to have a human agent bypass the OTP requirement and switch verification to email or an authenticator app, rather than using automated self-service flows that loop back to requiring the old number.
